why: A credential split with words between its pieces on one line. Accidents split a credential at a line break, which the line-joined view rejoins; words interleaved on one line are deliberate, and a deliberate author has encodings no view undoes. The cross-word view that caught this also refused ordinary English -- risk-based, task-queue -- and every agent whose identifier contained ask- (register D17).

why: A key whose line starts with its prefix, after a line ending in a letter, wrapped within its first sixteen characters. The line-joined view puts that letter before the prefix, so the anchored rule finds no word boundary. At any real wrap width the first line carries more than sixteen key characters and the identity view catches it; this shape needs a line narrower than the prefix plus sixteen.

A key split into adjacent string literals is joined by the language, not by a wrap: the quotes between the pieces are authored syntax, like the words in evade-secret-split. Policy D rejoins what a terminal or a mail client wrapped, and rejoining literals needs a model of each language's syntax (register D17).

The same authored split with an operator between the literals, recorded beside the adjacent-literal case so that a view rejoining one language's syntax is not read as covering the family (register D17).
A backslash continuation inside a key is typed, not wrapped: tools that wrap a long command break it between arguments, where the key stays whole. Policy D rejoins wraps (register D17).

A connection string wrapped inside its user or password is rejoined only by the line-joined view, which the URI rule no longer reads: its open classes made a host:port ending one line and a decorator, annotation or @-mention starting the next read as user:pass@. Unlike WebhookUrl's join, that false positive is ordinary code and the wrap it bought is rare, since a connection string is short (register D17).

R10.78 declines U+E0100 to U+E01EF: ordinary use is open (ideographic variation sequences in names). A run of selectors after one character carries one value each while ordinary text carries at most one; a run rule is a different kind of rule, so this evades and is recorded.
R10.78 declines U+034F: the combining grapheme joiner orders marks in Hebrew and Arabic, so its use is open. It splits the phrase for the pattern, and it evades.
R10.78 declines U+3164 and the other Hangul fillers: conjoining jamo for archaic syllables, and U+3164 pads blank names, so the use is open. It stands in for a space and evades.

The narrowed `pwd` form is a password only after a `;`, an opening quotation mark or a line start (R10.86). A command word and a space is none of them, so a real password assigned after one is let through; the same position rule is what lets `echo PWD=/build/output` pass.
Space-separated key=value pairs (the libpq and ODBC DSN form) put `pwd` after a space, which is not a position R10.86 accepts; the legacy rule refused it and the narrowed one does not.
A password may begin with `$`, `%`, `~` or `/`, and R10.86 reads a value that begins with one as a reference or a path; the legacy rule refused it and the narrowed one does not.
U+0085 survives SCREEN into the scanned views (it is deleted only in the line-joined view) and is not a line start for the `pwd` form, which knows LF and a lone CR (R10.86, amended 2026-10-29).
U+2028 survives SCREEN into the scanned views and is not a line start for the `pwd` form (R10.86, amended 2026-10-29).
U+2029 survives SCREEN into the scanned views and is not a line start for the `pwd` form (R10.86, amended 2026-10-29).

A URL query joins its pairs with `&`, which is not a position R10.86 accepts for `pwd` (a `;`, an opening quotation mark or a line start), so a password carried in a query string is let through; the same position rule is what lets a path or a reference after `pwd=` pass.
